there are at least three incentives for discrimination that the Commission can recognize and address: (1) transmission owners with generation affiliates have an incentive to favor the interconnection of large loads that agree to take service from their affiliated generation; (2) transmission owners have an incentive to favor large loads interconnecting in front of the meter to maximize transmission charges; and (3) incumbent utilities have an incentive to seek to develop the generation component of co-located load.

Utilities are already taking advantage of regulatory uncertainty to extract concessions from data centers.  A commitment from the Commission to act on transmission-level load interconnection would discipline utility action and help prevent undue discrimination.

letters.desc: AES supports FERC acting within its clear authority over transmission-level cost recovery but warns that asserting jurisdiction over historically state-jurisdictional retail interconnection processes would create disputes that delay, rather than speed, large-load connections. Retail electric service agreements are state-jurisdictional regardless of voltage level.
quotes: If the Commission asserts jurisdiction over load interconnection processes that have historically been state-jurisdictional or issues a standalone rulemaking without considering existing stakeholder efforts, then the ANOPR's objective of expediting large load interconnections in a non-discriminatory manner may be delayed.
AES respectfully recommends that the Commission develop a robust record and consider existing stakeholder and state initiatives before seeking to standardize large load interconnection.

agreements to provide retail electric service (regardless of whether such agreements involve service under a high voltage tariff) are state jurisdictional because (among other reasons) such service necessarily involves service over distribution facilities to the end user.

There is a clear role for the Commission in ensuring that certain cost-recovery mechanisms are just and reasonable (such as cost recovery related to the construction of network upgrades if a large load abandons the interconnection prior to taking retail service).

letters.desc: APGA argues the ANOPR's jurisdictional scope is too narrow because large electric loads powered by interstate gas pipelines fall within FERC's regulatory reach but are not addressed. The association asks FERC to evaluate whether and how such facilities affect interstate commerce and to bring natural gas infrastructure into the large-load framework.
quotes: APGA supports the Secretary's emphasis on public engagement in shaping this rulemaking process. However, we are concerned that the current scope of the ANOPR overlooks the critical role natural gas infrastructure plays in supporting large electric loads.

As AI data centers and other high-demand facilities continue to grow, many are relying on natural gas-fired generation to meet their energy needs. Because many of these gas-fired facilities may draw from interstate pipelines regulated by FERC, their energy use has implications for interstate commerce.
APGA requests that as the Commission contemplate jurisdiction over large loads, they consider how these large loads may influence interstate natural gas markets and infrastructure.
APGA urges the Commission to incorporate natural gas considerations into this rulemaking to support an energy future that safeguards the interests of public gas utilities and their customers.

letters.desc: CEBA takes no position on whether FERC has authority over large load interconnections but insists the Commission must clearly define jurisdictional limits in any rulemaking. The filing warns that a 20 MW threshold would pull state-regulated facilities into federal oversight, and that behind-the-meter systems must be explicitly excluded.
quotes: if the Commission proceeds with a rulemaking in this docket, it will be critical for the Commission to explicitly seek comment on and clearly define the boundaries of its jurisdiction to ensure that any final rule rests on a solid legal foundation and is well-understood by industry stakeholders.

A 20 MW cutoff, for example, is too low: it would capture many mid-sized industrial and commercial facilities (factories, hospitals, campuses) traditionally under state jurisdiction, creating tension with state regulators and blurring wholesale vs. retail boundaries.

Pulling these systems into new transmission-level regulatory frameworks would create confusion, raise costs, and slow deployment—not only harming local reliability but also increasing systemwide energy costs.

letters.desc: EEI argues that retail load interconnection has been regulated by states under the existing FPA framework and that FERC has not previously exercised jurisdiction in this space. EEI warns that asserting jurisdiction could raise major questions doctrine concerns and urges the Commission to advance reforms on sound jurisdictional footing.
quotes: interconnection service for retail end-use customers (including large load customers) is regulated by the states under the existing regulatory paradigm. Any Commission action must recognize that large load customers are end-use retail customers, meaning the delivery service they receive necessarily includes an element of local distribution service.

Reading the statute to take away authority from states that they have consistently applied, without a clear Congressional mandate to do so, may run afoul of the major questions doctrine and would be something the Commission must consider.

letters.desc: EEI urges FERC to craft federal policy that complements rather than displaces state regulatory processes, implying concern about federal action that could override the state tariff frameworks already in place across 29 states.
quotes: We continue to underscore the importance of crafting federal policies that build upon, rather than disrupt, existing forward progress, including state processes and stakeholder efforts.

letters.desc: ENGIE wants clear FERC jurisdiction to enable large load interconnection rules, but insists the final rule stay within federal authority and not encroach on state jurisdiction. Clear, legally defensible rules are treated as a prerequisite for long-term investment.
quotes: Reforms to PUHCA that allow IPPs to make direct sales to large loads without losing PUHCA exemptions for upstream owners would facilitate the interconnection and service of new large loads to the electric grid.
Permitting IPPs to file only one request, instead of individual requests for each transaction would greatly reduce the barriers to the development of hybrid large load interconnections.
Clear, consistent and legally defensible rules are essential for IPPs and all stakeholders to foster long-term investment and to bring large load interconnection to fruition.
One way to ensure validity and durability of the final rule is to respect and account for the limits of federal authority and avoid interfering with areas under state jurisdiction and control.

letters.org: Georgia Power CompanyAlabama Power CompanyMississippi Power Company ,
letters.desc: Southern Companies warn that several ANOPR proposals, including withdrawal rights for retail customers, an option to build transmission, and a federal cost-allocation standard for bundled-service jurisdictions, could intrude on state retail regulatory authority. They argue FERC should stay within established jurisdictional limits and issue rules that will survive legal challenge. They support federal action only where the Commission's authority is clear and where regional processes are not already working.
quotes: In the Southeast, the vertically-integrated nature of Southern Companies' operations, paired with pre-existing integrated planning procedures, enables Southern Companies to adapt quickly and provide the type of coordinated interconnection operations envisioned in the ANOPR.
Southern Companies respectfully urge the Commission to avoid implementing the ANOPR in a manner that would impede these successful existing processes.
if queue backlogs and procedural impediments exist in other parts of the country, the Commission may need to implement reforms of the type proposed in the ANOPR in those regions.
Instead of a one-size-fits-all approach, Southern Companies urge the Commission to focus its reforms where they are most needed to ensure affordability, reliability, and speed to market.
the Commission should craft rules applicable to specific regions or consider exempting regions that have demonstrated success in this area and do not need to adopt new rules.

As an alternative to prescriptive federal requirements, the Commission could achieve the objectives of the ANOPR by using lessons learned from this proceeding to establish a list of national best practices for large load interconnections and adopt a policy statement or similar vehicle to encourage the use of these best practices.

An end-use customer has no right to withdraw power from the grid without being subject to applicable state laws on retail energy use and applicable retail franchises, and Congress has unambiguously kept the Commission out of the business of retail regulation, respecting states' police powers.

the eighth reform principle, which suggests a new federal standard for how transmission costs should be allocated to large load retail customers, risks directly intruding on retail ratemaking in jurisdictions that have retained bundled retail service.

A new rule that greatly expands the Commission's jurisdiction—without factual support to support that expansion, especially in regions already achieving stated objectives—may impede rather than advance progress.

Southern Companies fully support the ANOPR's stated objectives of timely and orderly interconnection of large loads to the transmission system, while also respectfully urging the Commission to focus on legally durable solutions that would not disrupt the successful outcomes already being achieved in the Southeast.

letters.desc: Google accepts FERC's interconnection jurisdiction but cautions against overstating it. States retain exclusive authority over retail rates and must be actively involved in every large load interconnection. Google's preferred reforms cluster at the less contested end of the jurisdictional spectrum.
quotes: Although Google agrees that the Commission has jurisdiction over the actual interconnection of large loads to the transmission system, it is important not to overstate the practical impact of that conclusion in the broader context of large load integration issues. Because states have exclusive jurisdiction over the rates, terms, and conditions of retail sales, every large load interconnection in the country will require active state involvement.

The substantive reforms discussed above that Google is advocating for in this pleading fall on the relatively uncontroversial end of the spectrum. Accordingly, those reforms not only minimize strain on the existing grid, but they also minimize jurisdictional friction between the Commission and the states, which Google believes will further help ensure their effectiveness, particularly in the near term.

letters.org: Governor Josh Shapiro and Governor Glenn Youngkin
letters.desc: The governors accept that LLA interconnection has national security dimensions but insist states must retain significant authority. They explicitly endorse FERC's existing distinctions protecting state authority over retail sales, siting, and load facilities not directly on the transmission system.
quotes: we strongly believe it is essential for states to retain significant jurisdiction in this area, we recognize that the timely interconnection of certain LLAs is a matter of national security and national economic wellbeing.
we believe that the limit as proposed would substantially impact traditional state jurisdiction over loads.
We look forward to further public participation on what characteristics and size best serve to implicate shared state and federal jurisdiction in this regard.

letters.desc: The brief describes the central jurisdictional tension without taking a firm side. It notes that all nineteen state commissions that filed either opposed or expressed caution about federal expansion, while data center developers favor a stronger federal role. It flags that post-Chevron legal doctrine raises durability risks for any unilateral FERC assertion and suggests joint state-federal regulation may be the more durable path.
quotes: The dominant tension in the docket record is the contest between federal and state regulatory authority.
every one of the nineteen state public utility commissions that individually filed comments either opposed or expressed significant caution regarding the proposed expansion of federal authority.
durable solutions may require joint state-federal regulation rather than unilateral federal assertion of control.

Wyoming's PSC, overseeing what may be the single most disproportionately affected state in the nation, has not placed its perspective, its concerns, or its existing regulatory tools on the federal record.
For state regulators, the implication is that absence from the federal record is not neutrality.

The legal durability of any FERC action faces scrutiny under the major questions doctrine articulated in West Virginia v. EPA and the elimination of Chevron deference under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.

letters.org: Industrial Energy Consumers of America et al.
letters.desc: The filers acknowledge FERC has jurisdiction over transmission-level interconnections but insist it must not override state authority over retail ratemaking, new customer service applications, and distribution service. They support a FERC role limited to transmission system studies and optional fast-lane processes, not a mandatory federalized regime for all large loads.
quotes: mandating all new loads greater than 20 MW to go through a separate, new, federal process could cause significant negative impacts, including: disrupting existing processes; triggering confusion between state and federal organizations and regulators; creating business uncertainty; and diverting limited and scarce resources from staff at the Commission, at RTOs/ISOs, and at public utilities.

FERC must tread carefully to avoid intruding into state regulation over retail ratemaking, including new customer service applications, distribution service to end-use customers, and certain generation-related issues.

Regulations that affect processes currently managed at the state level could include a sunset provision, while regulations that are squarely focused on transmission grid transparency, load forecasting, and grid efficiency could be permanent reforms.

letters.org: Industrial Energy Consumers of America et al.
letters.desc: The filers support FERC authority over BES interconnection studies but insist state jurisdiction over retail service must be preserved. They propose an optional federal fast-lane as the way to add federal standardization without displacing state processes that are working. They prefer the Seven Factor Test over a fixed MW threshold to determine when FERC jurisdiction applies.
quotes: standardization of studies impacting the bulk electric system ("BES") is within FERC's jurisdiction, the comments affirm the importance of maintaining state jurisdiction over retail services provided to an end-use customer.

the Commission should consider implementing an optional and elective, fast lane, federal interconnection process, consistent with the framework in the initial comments of the Industrial Customer Organizations.

If FERC implements a standardized large load interconnection process and load queue, then the Commission should consider using FERC's Seven Factor Test to evaluate the jurisdictional nature of the interconnection, in lieu of any arbitrary MW threshold.

letters.desc: IECA urges collaboration between FERC and state regulators rather than jurisdictional conflict, but strongly opposes any mandatory federal process that overrides states where interconnection is already working. The filing sees joint cross-jurisdictional study as the solution in problem regions, with existing state processes preserved elsewhere.
quotes: Rather than spending valuable time fighting between the Commission and State regulators over jurisdictional boundaries, we urge all sides to work together to recognize and remedy those circumstances in which the process of interconnecting large loads to the interstate transmission system under State laws is taking an inordinate amount of time and seek ways to expedite the process for interconnecting large loads to the grid.

we also urge the Commission to recognize regional differences and not impose a new mandatory interconnection process on those regions experiencing rapid load growth from large loads, which are not experiencing interconnection challenges or delays.

We submit that a collaborative approach between States and the Commission can produce a process that can simultaneously study both a Data Center and a contractually-associated electric generation resource by joining both (i) the Federal approval of interconnection of the generation resource (through the Commission-regulated LGIP and LGIA process) and (ii) the State approval (through a State-regulated utility) of the interconnection of a new large load.

we suggest that any load interconnection program that the Commission may introduce should not be mandatory across the entirety of the U.S., i.e., a one-size-fits-all approach is not the best way forward.

letters.org: Massachusetts Office of the Attorney General
letters.desc: The State Entities note that FERC has not historically regulated load interconnections and that legal precedent for the claimed jurisdiction is thin. They support FERC clarifying a basis for jurisdiction over transmission interconnections but insist any rule be narrowly tailored to avoid encroaching on state authority over distribution and retail ratemaking. They also want the rule to leave room for states and RTOs to build on federal baselines.
quotes: there does not appear to be legal precedent directly granting this jurisdiction, even when limited to transmission interconnections.
the Commission must establish clear jurisdictional boundaries that appropriately respect state jurisdictional authority over the distribution system and retail ratemaking.

the Commission's rulemaking must be carefully designed and narrowly tailored to avoid an expansion of this jurisdiction over end-use customer loads interconnecting to the local electric distribution system.
the Commission should clearly define the scope of this rulemaking.
different regions across the country should be allowed to build upon federal standards to create rules that address unique regional challenges and opportunities.
any Commission rulemaking here should not impede that progress or prevent other regions from making similar progress.

letters.desc: MISO raises concerns that large load interconnection may involve retail electricity sales outside FERC's authority, and that federal rules could conflict with existing state commissions that already oversee load-serving entities. MISO does not deny FERC has some authority, but urges caution about displacing state and member roles.
quotes: Fundamentally, MISO questions whether standardized large load interconnection procedures will result in the "speed to power" that is necessary to allow the United States to effectively compete in the global competition for economic development, such as in artificial intelligence and creating manufacturing and industrial jobs.

In lieu of requiring standard large load interconnection procedures, and in light of the concerns expressed above, the Commission should allow MISO, as well as other industry participants, to continue focusing attention on efficiently interconnecting large loads pursuant to processes that reflect the unique circumstances of their members, states, stakeholders, and transmission systems.

Alternatively, the Commission could refine the principles started by DOE and issue a policy statement to guide the industry processes to be used for large load interconnections.  This would enable Transmission Providers to craft unique solutions suited for their regions guided by Commission principles.

To the extent the Commission believes it must pursue standard large load interconnection procedures or another rule mandate through a formal rulemaking process, it should extend the "Independent Entity Variation" principle to any final rule.

there is no evidence of undue discrimination of loads, large or small, by load serving utilities.  Unlike generators, individual load additions can site where they want and are not assigned costs for their impacts to the transmission system at a wholesale level.
Creating a parallel set of provisions at the federal level will likely result in confusion and may create opportunities for forum shopping.

bulk power system owners, operators, and users must register with NERC to ensure compliance with mandatory reliability standards.  This includes generators.  However, loads are not currently required to register with NERC.  Therefore, there would currently be no responsibility or accountability for loads that build interconnection facilities or network upgrades.  Consequently, MISO views this principle as impractical.

letters.desc: Missouri PSC supports FERC asserting jurisdiction over transmission interconnections but insists it must stay within the FPA's bright line. The commission warns that FERC has not explained how existing practices are discriminatory, must demonstrate clear congressional authorization, and cannot commandeer state authority over resource planning, retail rates, or generation siting.
quotes: FERC must point to 'clear congressional authorization' for the power it claims to exercise.

The ANOPR does not explain whether, or how, current state and RTO interconnection practices are discriminatory or unjust or unreasonable. Unlike generation, load represents an opportunity for a utility to increase revenue, not competition.

FERC must narrowly tailor its final rule so as not to conflict with the vertically integrated structure maintained in Missouri and other states. A final rule cannot commandeer state authority over resource planning or the construction and siting of large loads and generation.

FERC cannot override states' own regulatory and economic development choices, or force state utility ratepayers to construct generation that is not planned for and approved under state IRP and certificate proceedings.

As Missouri and other state commissions confront issues of affordability in both wholesale and retail electricity rates, FERC must ensure that costs under its jurisdiction are allocated in a just and reasonable manner, and that other customers do not unjustly subsidize the energy needs of large load customers.
In developing its final rule, FERC should look to the states as partners, not obstacles.

letters.org: National Association of State Utility Consumer Advocates
letters.desc: Consumer advocates and state entities find no clear legal precedent for FERC's proposed jurisdictional expansion over large load interconnections. Any assertion of jurisdiction must be carefully bounded to transmission facilities and must not displace state authority over retail cost recovery, distribution interconnections, or retail tariffs.
quotes: there does not appear to be legal precedent directly granting this jurisdiction, even when limited to transmission interconnections.

FERC should address whether and how it has jurisdiction over 'interconnections directly to transmission facilities.'  If FERC finds that it has jurisdiction, the second issue is how to define 'transmission facilities' to avoid infringing on state authority over the distribution system.
any extension of federal jurisdiction should ensure that large loads are currently and remain subject to state jurisdiction regarding the recovery and allocation of retail costs.
establishing unprecedented federal jurisdiction and new large load interconnection rules is likely to have sweeping impacts on the nation's ratepayers and electric grids.

FERC's implementation of the ANOPR should not preempt these salutary efforts underway at the State level directed at resolving many of the problems targeted by the ANOPR if they exceed a minimum level of standards that may emanate from FERC's implementation of the fourth principle of the ANOPR.

letters.desc: National Grid accepts that FERC may assert FPA jurisdiction over large load interconnections but insists that authority be confined to transmission interconnection requirements. State control over retail service rates and conditions must remain undisturbed. Federal oversight should accelerate state objectives, not override them.
quotes: Federal jurisdiction over large load interconnections to the transmission grid should be positioned as an accelerant to State objectives.  Assertion of FPA jurisdiction should be done in a manner that is narrowly tailored to interconnection as proposed in the ANOPR, so that the Commission's narrow jurisdiction over large load interconnection does not interfere with State jurisdiction over retail service while enabling collaboration that benefits customers and the grid.

letters.desc: NRECA supports Commission action on large-load interconnections only if it stays within the FPA's limits. Any new rules cannot override state and local authority over retail rates and service territories, cannot mandate wheeling to ultimate consumers, and cannot become a vehicle for retail competition.
quotes: any Commission assertion of jurisdiction over large-load interconnections must conform to the terms of the jurisdiction granted the Commission by section 201 of the FPA and thus cannot impinge on the jurisdiction of state and local electric regulatory authorities over the rates, terms, and conditions of retail electric sales to such large loads.
the FPA prohibits a Commission order that is inconsistent with state law governing retail marketing areas or that requires the transmission of electric energy directly to an ultimate consumer.
federal interconnection procedures for large loads are not, and cannot be, a backdoor route to retail competition. State and local regulators determine the terms of retail direct access.

letters.desc: NERC supports Commission action on large loads but insists any resulting order reference the full Bulk Power System, not just the Bulk Electric System subset. NERC declines to weigh in on FERC's jurisdiction under sections other than 215 and notes that large load users are potential BPS users under existing precedent. The stance is mixed because NERC supports the proceeding while also correcting what it sees as a jurisdictional misdescription in the ANOPR.
quotes: NERC requests that any ensuing Commission action accurately reflects the scope of NERC's reliability authority, which statutorily extends to Reliability Standards that provide for the reliable operation of the BPS and is distinguished from the Commission's jurisdiction regarding the transmission and sale of electric energy.

NERC declines to comment on matters outside its purview, such as the proposed ANOPR assertions regarding the Commission's jurisdiction under other provisions of the Federal Power Act, including section 205.
Among the Secretary's proposed principles is a proposal that 'utilities serving large loads must meet all applicable NERC reliability standards….'

there is opportunity to further clarify NERC's authority as the ERO under section 215, because one of the proposed ANOPR principles suggest that NERC's registration categories and Reliability Standards are to ensure the 'reliability of the BES.'
NERC requests out of an abundance of caution that any subsequent Commission action in this proceeding reflects the full scope of NERC's reliability authority as pertaining to the BPS.

NERC currently has limited registry criteria applicable to 'users' of the BPS. Nevertheless, FERC precedent and legislative history of the Federal Power Act indicate that users of the BPS mean all those who 'use' the BPS.

FERC stated its concerns that, '[under NERC's proposed definition] a large industrial customer that receives electric energy directly from the [BPS] may not be defined as a user of the BPS, even though it may directly affect the reliability of the [BPS].'

Although NERC has not developed any criteria that would add large load entities to the NCR at this time, NERC requests that any resulting Commission action reflect NERC's scope of statutory authority as the ERO to ensure the reliability of the BPS.

letters.desc: ODEC supports FERC exercising jurisdiction over large-load interconnections but opposes a bright-line rule tied to facility labels or voltage. It argues the Order 888 seven-factor functional analysis should govern because cooperative distribution facilities often serve as the physical connection point between large loads and the transmission system.
quotes: ODEC does not support a brightline rule that the Commission's jurisdiction should be limited to interconnections directly to only those facilities that have been labeled or characterized as "transmission facilities."
the Commission should adopt the same approach for large-load interconnections

letters.desc: PG&E argues that FERC's authority under the FPA does not extend to retail electric service, retail rate design, or certain co-location matters, and urges the Commission to respect state regulatory zones. At the same time, it says states must not indefinitely delay action in areas where the Commission grants them flexibility.
quotes: PG&E believes that three key principles are essential to any final Commission rule: Protecting existing ratepayers from incurring additional or stranded costs while also adopting fair and equitable cost responsibility and allocation approaches for large load customers; Appropriately balancing state and Commission jurisdiction and developing a complimentary and cooperative framework, while also ensuring timely state action on large load issues; and Developing clear rules that will expedite large load interconnections by allowing flexibility rather than imposing additional requirements that slow the interconnection process.
the Commission should consider FPA limitations on retail electric sales issues as well as matters that are subject to state jurisdiction.

any final rule should be consistent with the Commission's determination earlier this year 'the states get to determine which entities are legally permitted to provide electricity to retail customers in co-location arrangements. The states also get to determine how the wholesale costs of providing electricity to those retail customers are recovered through retail rates.'

the Commission should be mindful that 'the Commission and states each regulate within separate zones of exclusive jurisdiction, with the states retaining authority over those matters not expressly conveyed to the Commission under the FPA.'

the Commission should also be clear in a final rule that, where flexibility is available, the states cannot indefinitely delay action. To the extent a state fails to act or provide clear guidance and rules by the implementation deadline, a utility should be able to submit a Section 205 filing to the Commission proposing tariff provisions for that utility that are consistent with the Commission's decision.

letters.org: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer AdvocateDelaware Division of the Public Advocate
letters.desc: The filers support FERC jurisdiction over interstate transmission and wholesale markets but strongly oppose any preemption of state authority over end-use customer interconnection and local distribution facilities. They cite Order 888, the FPA's explicit reservations, Loper Bright, and the Major Questions Doctrine as reasons a broad jurisdictional assertion would face serious legal risk.
quotes: The Joint Consumer Advocates support jurisdictional federal avenues for regulating the interstate transmission and wholesale market aspects of large load interconnection, while respecting states' existing authority, including the authority to interconnect large loads at the distribution level.
FERC has never claimed the kind of jurisdiction over end-use customer interconnection that the ANOPR proposes.
The ANOPR risks lengthy, burdensome, and meritorious legal challenges to the extent that it ignores the FPA's and FERC's explicit acknowledgements of state jurisdiction.

A FERC final rule that includes federal preemption of any existing, traditional state authority will face an uphill battle under the U.S. Supreme Court's new standard of review for agency statutory interpretation.

letters.desc: PJM acknowledges federal interest in large load interconnection but warns that displacing EDCs and TOs from retail-jurisdictional processes risks prolonged litigation that would delay rather than advance the ANOPR's goals. PJM urges FERC to act on issues squarely within its existing wholesale jurisdiction first.
quotes: While the prospect of a federally-regulated large load interconnection process warrants further exploration, PJM encourages FERC to seize available opportunities to issue nearer-term regulatory guidance on matters squarely within its wholesale and transmission jurisdiction about:  resource adequacy, the provision of ancillary services, mandatory operational regimes, potential wholesale rate classes for different types of load customers, interconnection and transmission planning, cost allocation, and NERC and Tariff reliability obligations and requirements.

It would be a significant development if FERC would not continue to allow local Electric Distribution Companies (EDCs) and Transmission Owners (TOs) to administer load interconnection processes subject to retail regimes and the traditional federal/wholesale-state/retail division of labor that has long characterized this space.

there remains a question as to whether any rule developed on the existing record targeted at this specific topic would entangle the Commission and stakeholders in a potentially contentious dispute that would distract from the need to provide a durable pathway to the ANOPR's desired outcome:  timely and orderly large load interconnections.

questions would need to be answered about whether such a new process will necessarily lead to different or enhanced large load interconnection results, and whether the theoretical benefits of a federally-regulated large load interconnection process outweigh the challenges of creating and administering a load queue at the RTO/ISO level.

letters.desc: PFT acknowledges FERC has some authority over transmission-level interconnection in RTO/ISO footprints but warns that DOE's proposal risks expanding that authority into retail service territory reserved to states. The filer stresses that loads and generators are fundamentally different and that the Federal Power Act does not authorize FERC to regulate the bundled retail services large loads seek. Federal action should stay within those limits.
quotes: Facilitating expeditious interconnection of these new customers is an important goal, but the proposal raises key questions about FERC's jurisdiction and, ultimately, could exacerbate the challenges of new large loads: speedy interconnection without expanding supply will strain reliability further and increase costs for all.

PFT respectfully urges the Commission to: (1) recognize the vital state regulatory role in effectively managing and serving large loads, overseeing intrastate transmission, and determining cost allocation; and (2) cautiously examine its jurisdictional authority so as to remain within the bounds of the law and preserve states' jurisdiction to continue to develop and deploy successful approaches to the large load challenge.

While large load interconnection presents challenges nationwide, the nature and severity of these challenges vary dramatically based on regional market structure and the effectiveness of state regulatory oversight.
Generators seek access to wholesale markets, within FERC's jurisdiction, but large loads seek to interconnect to obtain bundled retail services, within states' jurisdiction.

DOE's assertion that transmission service encompasses 'the appurtenant benefits of such' threatens state jurisdiction to the extent that new large loads could, for example, argue that failure to provide them energy and capacity is a violation of the terms of their interconnection or entitles them to direct access to wholesale markets.

FERC should avoid taking action or asserting jurisdiction in such a way that would serve as an effective preemption of large load interconnection through DOE Section 403 authority or sweeping changes to FERC-jurisdictional interconnection procedures could disrupt effective state regulation without corresponding benefits in jurisdictions where state processes work well.

DOE and FERC could consider, for example, establishing safe harbor provisions whereby states demonstrating effective management of large load interconnection remain free from federal procedural mandates or that encourage states to continue to holistically solve the interrelated challenges of interconnection of large loads and critical new generation.

letters.desc: PPL acknowledges that federal jurisdiction may be needed where states obstruct large load interconnection, but argues its own state processes in Pennsylvania and Kentucky work well and have not delayed any project. PPL proposes that FERC create a triggered federal backstop, available only when a state process stalls, modeled on the IIJA transmission siting provisions.
quotes: By asserting federal jurisdiction, FERC would displace not just longstanding state jurisdiction, but the detailed processes, practices, agreements, and precedents developed over decades in each state to answer the myriad and intricate questions of retail load interconnection.
In some parts of the country, this assertion of jurisdiction may be necessary to accelerate the interconnection of these crucial loads. In others, it may instead slow them significantly.

Pennsylvania's efficient oversight has not added a single day to any data center development timeline. Each site is proceeding as quickly as possible given broader issues such as land acquisition/permitting and global supply chains for necessary components.
FERC could create a federal backstop for large load interconnections that the utility, or potentially the customer, could trigger when a state process bogs down.

letters.desc: RSI does not dispute FERC's authority but opposes expanding it as the ANOPR envisions. The filer argues the six-month deadline is too short, the evidentiary record is insufficient, and FERC should restrict new federal oversight to load configurations that also participate in wholesale markets, leaving purely retail load interconnections to states.
quotes: six months is not a "reasonable time" and is insufficient for FERC to consider, and for parties to meaningfully participate in, a rulemaking that expands the Commission's exertion of jurisdiction.
The proposed ANOPR does not provide FERC sufficient evidence or support to issue a NOPR and final rule in the way envisioned.

The Commission should make no substantive decision by April 30, 2026, and instead seek more information in a separate proceeding, rather than issue a rule that makes the problems in the bulk electric system worse.

the Commission could initiate one or more joint boards under section 209 of the Federal Power Act. These joint boards could be broken out by market or planning region, and could resemble the joint boards of state and federal regulators created nearly 20 years ago on security-constrained economic dispatch, or SCED.
comparison of large loads connecting at the transmission level to large generators connecting to transmission is incongruent.

Getting FERC involved in the interconnection of customers that only seek to take a state-jurisdictional end-use service, simply because they are connecting to the bulk electric system, is nonsensical in the context of DOE's proposed ANOPR.

FERC should conduct a rulemaking permitting Commission-jurisdictional interconnection processes for load, but only where the interconnection is necessary to offer or receive an otherwise wholesale market service.

delineating the applicability of a federalized agreement and process based on the interaction with wholesale markets keeps the Commission from having to make arbitrary determinations. As such, RSI's proposal would be available to any size load, as long as they meet the other criteria for its applicability

Limiting the applicability of a rulemaking to those processes that are already FERC-jurisdictional (i.e. expanding the LGIA concept to others seeking to connect to the transmission grid to participate in wholesale markets) reduces the novelty of an ultimate rule, maintains the current balance between state and federal oversight, reduces litigation risk, and ensures that resource adequacy concerns with the rule (that load will take power before generation can catch up) are mitigated
Cooperative federalism harmonizes state and federal policies and avoids working at cross-purposes.

letters.desc: SEIA supports the Commission issuing a rulemaking but finds the first three jurisdictional theories in the ANOPR legally weak. SEIA argues the generator-interconnection analogy fails because loads are customers, not competitors, and that the 'affecting rates' theory extends jurisdiction too broadly. SEIA backs the fourth theory, Commission authority over transmission in interstate commerce, but only when loads connect directly to transmission under the seven-factor test and subject to state boundary limits.
quotes: SEIA agrees that the Commission has the authority to issue a rulemaking to standardize the process for interconnecting large loads to the transmission system and urges the Commission to do so while recognizing state jurisdictional boundaries.

Large loads, however, are not competitors to transmission-owning utilities; they are customers. Transmission Owners are financially motivated to attract large loads to their service territories and to provide favorable interconnection terms and conditions.

Any final rule in this proceeding must clearly limit jurisdiction to the interconnection of large loads to the Commission-jurisdictional transmission system, as defined under the Commission's seven-factor test.

letters.desc: SPP cautions that an option-to-build right for large load customers may conflict with state laws restricting who may own transmission. SPP's tariff allows only eligible transmission customers to be assigned network upgrades.
quotes: the Commission should be mindful of state laws that restrict who can build and own transmission. Network Upgrades assigned through SPP's transmission service process can only be assigned to entities that request transmission service.

letters.org: Utility Intervention Unit, New York State Department of Stat
letters.desc: The UIU supports FERC taking action but warns that a single national standard could override NYISO's existing, vetted processes and create conflicting timelines and cost-responsibility determinations. It asks that any new rules allow regions to seek variations rather than imposing uniform federal procedures.
quotes: Any new large load rules should be built upon NYISO's established interconnection processes, manuals, and datasets rather than overriding them.

Creating a national standard could introduce confusion, conflicting study timelines, or inconsistent cost-responsibility determinations at a time when speed in the interconnection process is needed most.

letters.desc: ACP opposes federal overreach in load interconnection, arguing it has been a state matter and cautioning that jurisdictional changes could jeopardize ongoing projects and increase delays. Prefers a state-driven approach with federal action as a backstop only when needed.
quotes: A state-driven approach, which would seek to minimize disruption of the multiple large load projects under development and seeking to interconnect today.
Any jurisdictional changes could jeopardize interconnection requests that are in process, and inadvertently increase interconnection delays.

letters.desc: The APSC warns that assigning large-load interconnection authority to FERC blurs the line between retail service and transmission, conflicts with Arkansas's vertically integrated utility model, and creates uncertainty about the obligation to serve. FERC should act only as a backstop where regional processes fail.
quotes: Federal action should be reserved for regions where processes are failing, not those where reforms are already in place and producing results.

Reassigning interconnection authority for large loads to FERC would blur the distinction between retail service and transmission interconnection, complicate state‑regulated special‑rate contracts, create uncertainty regarding which entity bears the obligation to serve, and risk conflict with the state's legislative framework.
Creating a system where the load is separated from the obligation to serve would result in the very thing the ANOPR seeks to avoid: making the grid less reliable.

the APSC urges FERC to support the state regulatory authorities by establishing voluntary best practices, establish backstop authority only in instances of demonstrated delay or discrimination, and avoid any implication that the federal government is asserting jurisdiction over retail‑level obligations.
A federal rule that overrides or duplicates these efforts is unnecessary and counterproductive.

letters.desc: The CPUC argues that large load interconnection is a retail transaction governed by state authority under the FPA, not a wholesale transmission matter for FERC. FERC's claimed analogies to generator interconnection and wholesale rate authority do not justify jurisdiction over retail end-use customers. States have existing proceedings and expertise and should retain control.
quotes: the CPUC objects to the Secretary of Energy's proposition that the proposed rules do not venture into state jurisdiction.
Large load interconnection is part of retail service and is not part of the transmission system operation or a purchase of wholesale electricity.
This analogy between generator and large-load interconnections is too simplistic and does not account for fundamental jurisdictional and technical distinctions established under the FPA.

States, including California, are already underway in addressing the concerns the Department of Energy identifies, making broad federal intervention duplicative and counter to the goal of timely energization of load.

the Commission should defer to rulemakings already underway by state regulators and, further, provide the opportunity for states to implement rules and regulations in the future to ensure the timely and cost-effective energization of large load and hybrid facilities
oversight of interconnecting large retail load customers to the transmission grid should remain under the domain of the states.

letters.desc: The CPUC argues the ANOPR exceeds FERC authority under the FPA. Retail load energization is not a wholesale transaction, FPA section 212(h) bars retail wheeling mandates, and Commission precedent reserves such matters to states. Expanding federal jurisdiction risks reclassifying distribution assets as transmission and forcing retail unbundling.
quotes: the proposed rulemaking, as described in the ANOPR, would extend beyond FERC's jurisdiction and undermine the system of cooperative federalism set forth in the Federal Power Act and amendments in the Energy Policy Act of 2005 ("FPA").

The Commission and the states have separate zones of exclusive jurisdiction.  Critically, and key to the analysis here, the states retain authority over matters not expressly granted to the Commission under the FPA.
This type of indirect impact is beyond the scope of the Commission's jurisdiction under the Federal Power Act.

FPA section 212(h) prohibits FERC from directing the provision of transmission directly to end users (retail wheeling).  The FPA reservation of jurisdiction over retail rates and services to the states includes retail load energization.
The terms of large load energization are not a sale of electric energy at wholesale and therefore fall into the "any other" category reserved for the states.
expansion in Federal jurisdiction would lead to confusion and likely conflict between federal regulation and state-approved tariffs.

FERC has consistently recognized, including in Order Nos. 2003 and 2023, that interconnection service is distinct from transmission service.  Yet under the ANOPR's reasoning, the act of connecting a large retail customer directly to transmission facilities could transform that retail delivery into a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale transaction – redefining distribution facilities and costs as transmission assets, shifting oversight of distribution expansion, maintenance, and rate recovery from state commissions to FERC.

either this process would slow energization of large load and extend the timeline for bringing AI data centers online, or these questions would go unaddressed, resulting in unreasonable cost-shifting and a less reliable electric grid for all.

"Given the magnitude of the request and the importance of the issues implicated by that request, it would be patently unreasonable and bad public policy for FERC to use an expedited process to expand its jurisdiction."

letters.desc: Fisher argues that physically islanded CRE networks should be explicitly exempt from FERC jurisdiction and NERC reliability standards. He flags statutory ambiguity in FPA Section 215 that could sweep in CRE utilities, and asks FERC and DOE to issue clarifying guidance confirming these systems are outside federal oversight.
quotes: I urge the Commission to enable Consumer Regulated Electricity (CRE), which offers a parallel path to timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory access to electricity for large loads.

The key advantage of CRE lies in eliminating the delays and regulatory risks associated with federal and state approval processes by ensuring there is no physical connection to electricity systems regulated by FERC or state commissions.
I urge the Commission to consider clarifying that any physically islanded network—with no connection whatsoever to the broader grid—is exempt from Commission oversight and NERC standards.

by my reading of Section 215 of the Federal Power Act, some CRE utilities could be deemed (inappropriately) to be part of the bulk power system based on the facility's (1) economic significance, (2) potential use of other connected networks, including fuel supply chains, or (3) electric equipment operating at high voltages.
The reliability of the bulk power system is best served by allowing FERC and NERC to focus on the interconnected regions and networks that serve residential customers.

Commission oversight over CRE utilities would be unnecessary and represent a departure from the intent of Section 215 of the Federal Power Act, which was to prevent wide-scale, cascading outages on the bulk power system like the one experienced in August 2003 in the Northeast United States.

DOE can use its existing authorities—without new legislation—to enable CRE by issuing clarifying guidance and model policy templates that: Clarify that CRE utilities are non-jurisdictional to FERC and NERC because they are not interconnected to the bulk electric system.
Issue a DOE–FERC joint policy statement confirming that islanded CRE utilities serving captive loads are not public utilities under the Federal Power Act or NERC jurisdiction.

letters.desc: Consumers Energy argues that asserting federal jurisdiction over large load interconnection as open-access transmission service is a departure from historical practice and risks encroaching on the states' authority over retail electric sales. The filer asks FERC to confirm that any jurisdictional action will not alter the retail classification of sales to large load customers or create undue preference.
quotes: interconnection of retail load has not, in the past, been considered to be a 'critical component of open access transmission service.' If the Commission decides to assert such jurisdiction, it would be an untested departure from historical practice.

the Commission should clarify that any potential assertion of Commission jurisdiction over the interconnection of large load customers to the transmission system will not change the retail nature of sales to such customers or result in undue preference to them.

not prejudging the best approach to advancing goals set forth in the ANOPR may mean that the Commission determines that a sweeping federal rule is not the best path forward, particularly if it may frustrate state initiatives that are currently in place or being developed.

letters.desc: The filing opposes FERC asserting jurisdiction over large load interconnections, arguing that the Federal Power Act reserves retail service authority to the states. Load interconnections involve end-user retail customers and are inherently tied to state-regulated functions, making them fundamentally different from generator interconnections. The company warns that federal overreach will trigger protracted litigation and harm policy goals, and if FERC proceeds, recommends limiting jurisdiction to transmission facilities using the existing seven-factor test rather than adopting new bright-line frameworks.
quotes: the Commission should take care to avoid asserting the authority to regulate matters that the Federal Power Act ("FPA") has reserved to the States.
the FPA makes clear that the Commission's jurisdiction extends "only to those matters which are not subject to regulation by the States."
To uphold any new Commission regulation, a court "must determine that it does not regulate retail electricity sales," which the FPA has reserved as "a job for the States alone."
the ANOPR proposal to regulate large load interconnections to the transmission system is, at best, on shaky jurisdictional ground.

Unlike generator interconnections, load interconnections involve the provision of electric service to end-user consumers (i.e., retail customers), making the generator interconnection process inapposite as a jurisdictional matter.
the receipt of energy by large load is inherently tied to retail distribution and state-regulated functions.

The extent of the Commission's authority to regulate load interconnections is murky at best and will undoubtedly be the subject of protracted litigation should the Commission decide to move forward with the ANOPR proposal.

any attempt by the Commission to expand its jurisdictional reach into that reserved to the States would be a serious and unnecessary misstep that may hamper achievement of the Administration's stated goals.
Consumers Energy respectfully requests that the Commission limit its assertion of jurisdiction to interconnections to transmission facilities, as defined by FERC's longstanding seven-factor test.

The Commission should continue to rely on its seven-factor test when determining whether a proposed interconnection concerns a FERC-jurisdictional transmission line or a state-jurisdictional distribution facility.
Adopting a new framework, such as a bright-line rule based on voltage or some other metric, would arbitrarily upend decades of Commission precedent and could have unintended consequences.
the Commission's seven-factor test should not be cast aside or revised to bootstrap Commission jurisdiction over large load interconnections.

letters.desc: EEI opposes expanding Commission jurisdiction over large load interconnection service, arguing that cooperative federalism and state authority are the appropriate framework. EEI contends there is no evidence of utility discrimination against large loads and that jurisdictional expansion would trigger litigation and leave reliability and resource adequacy questions unanswered.
quotes: EEI members share the Administration's goal of enabling speed-to-power for large load customers.  We urge the Commission to move deliberately forward in a manner that protects other customers, ensures grid reliability, and acknowledges the distinct role of the states.
The strongest path forward is through adherence to principles of cooperative federalism.

An overwhelming majority of commenters, representing a diverse array of perspectives, agree that the Commission should avoid disrupting processes already in place that are supported by the utilities, have been approved by state regulatory authorities, and underlie large load customers' investment decisions.
Most commenters support the Commission achieving the DOE ANOPR goals through cooperative federalism, without upending the existing jurisdictional paradigm.

Given the speed with which many states and utilities have adopted large load policies and programs, it would be counterproductive for the Commission to push the pause button and spend months or years developing Commission-jurisdictional uniform large load interconnection procedures.

Any new assertion of Commission jurisdiction to large load interconnection service will raise innumerable questions, such as who would be responsible for serving the load or maintaining reliability and resource adequacy over time.

There is no merit to allegations that utilities are delaying the interconnection of large loads to the transmission system.  There is simply no incentive to do so and in fact, as the record demonstrates, there is every incentive for utilities to work with large load customers and states to find ways to bring large loads on as quickly as reliably possible.

letters.desc: Entergy argues FERC lacks the evidentiary basis for a nationwide rule because no substantial evidence shows large load interconnections in MISO or the Entergy Operating Companies' territories are unjust or discriminatory. Regional differences mean complaints from one RTO cannot be generalized nationally. State and retail regulators retain authority over retail supply arrangements.
quotes: the evidence here does not support Commission action on a nationwide basis
the Commission cannot automatically extrapolate specific claims made about load interconnections in one area to other parts of the country

there is no evidence that would support a finding that load interconnections in MISO generally, or the service territories of the Entergy Operating Companies specifically, are unjust, unreasonable, or unduly discriminatory or preferential

the Commission should not adopt the requests of some Commenters asking the Commission to adopt standardized rules across the country and to require that such rules be included in pro forma procedures that would be filed with the Commission
the Commission should not use a new load interconnection rule to substitute its judgment for that of state regulators about what constitutes reliable retail supply arrangements

letters.desc: Exelon warns that modeling large load interconnection rules on Order No. 2003 is legally and practically risky. Load interconnection differs from generation interconnection in fundamental ways, jurisdictional disputes are likely, and Order No. 2003 itself took over five years to finalize and still has not resolved underlying problems after 24 years.
quotes: Order No. 2003, as the Commission is aware, took more than five years to progress from the initial ANOPR (October 2001) to the end of the appeal process (January 2007). Even on an accelerated timeline, Commission action here could extend compliance well into the next presidential administration, and the jurisdictional issues are likely to be vigorously litigated as well.
it has been 24 years since the Commission commenced the proposed rulemaking that led to Order No. 2003 and we are still working to resolve the shortcomings of that rule.

letters.desc: The GPSC argues that federal intervention is unnecessary in Georgia because the vertically integrated market structure gives the state commission full oversight over large load interconnection. It acknowledges other market structures may need FERC action but urges no further federal involvement in Georgia.
quotes: The GPSC affirms that it is best positioned to ensure the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads with its current policy and regulatory tools.
The vertically integrated market structure in Georgia allows the GPSC to oversee every facet of this load growth and adjust to market conditions as they emerge.
The GPSC understands that states in other market structures may require different interventions from FERC.
The GPSC will continue to collaborate towards shared goals without the need for further Federal action in Georgia.

letters.desc: The IEA opposes FERC assertion of jurisdiction over retail load interconnections, arguing that the Federal Power Act limits FERC to wholesale sales and transmission in interstate commerce, explicitly excluding facilities used in local distribution. The filer contends that load interconnections for retail customers fundamentally differ from generator interconnections (no discrimination risk), that states have effectively regulated retail interconnections for decades, and that Section 212 of the FPA prohibits conditioning transmission on service to ultimate customers. The final rule must explicitly exclude retail service from federal jurisdiction to avoid conflicts with established state cost recovery mechanisms.
quotes: However, as noted in NARUC's November 11, 2025 resolution on this topic, the ANOPR raises important questions about jurisdictional boundaries under the Federal Power Act ("FPA"), which sets out clear delineations of federal and state regulatory authority. Moreover, states such as Indiana are demonstrating that state procedures are proactively and effectively addressing new large load customer interconnections, rendering significant FERC intrusions into state jurisdiction unnecessary and potentially duplicative.

Recognizes that states are proactively addressing large load customer issues. Preserves state jurisdiction over service to, and rates for, retail customers (of all magnitudes) and local distribution facilities.

In addition, for decades the IEA electric utilities have used individualized electric service contracts, approved by the IURC, to address electric interconnection and power supply to large, sophisticated customers. As noted above, the 2024 Indiana legislation also provides for expedited IURC approvals of such individualized contracts which can be customized to meet the unique needs of both the customers and the utilities. While the ANOPR asserts a desire to standardize large load customer interconnections, the IEA respectfully submits that unique contracts between a utility and its large load retail customers, scrutinized by state regulators, will better serve the large load customers, the utility, and the utility's other retail customers.

The ANOPR asserts that large load interconnections are a "critical component of open access transmission service," like electric generator interconnections standardized in Order No. 2003, requiring minimum terms and conditions to ensure non-discriminatory transmission service. There are significant differences, however, between electric generator connections and large load retail customer interconnections, particularly in traditionally-regulated, vertically-integrated states like Indiana. Not only are there longstanding federal and state jurisdictional differences between electric generator interconnections and retail customer interconnections, there are also differences in the potential for discrimination. Transmission service to independent electric generators raises legitimate questions of discrimination for competitive reasons. In contrast, in states like Indiana, utilities have both an obligation and a natural incentive to serve (and interconnect) new customers.

Transmission interconnections for all retail customers, regardless of size, are part and parcel of a utility's provision of retail utility service. States have adequately and efficiently regulated interconnections between their jurisdictional utilities and large load customers for decades. The only difference today is the number of large load customers — mostly data centers — seeking to interconnect and take service. A change in the number of large retail customers seeking interconnection should not drive a major change in jurisdictional boundaries between the federal government and states.

The ANOPR also asserts that large load interconnections directly affect wholesale electricity rates, over which the FERC has exclusive jurisdiction under the FPA to ensure wholesale rates are just and reasonable. But the FERC cannot use its "affecting" jurisdiction to regulate where the Federal Power Act has expressly denied FERC jurisdiction. Notably, section 212 of the FPA provides that "[n]o order issued under this chapter shall be conditioned upon or require the transmission of electric energy: (1) directly to an ultimate customer …." 16 U.S. Code § 824k(h). Moreover, the impact of large load interconnections affects state retail electricity rates more than wholesale rates. In Indiana, the IEA electric utilities devote the vast majority of their investments and operations to serving their retail customers, not wholesale customers. States such as Indiana are experienced and well-positioned to ensure that all cost components of a utility's retail electric service, including transmission interconnections, translate into just and reasonable retail rates.

States — including Indiana — have long regulated the interconnection of retail customers, cost recovery for upgrades, local reliability planning, and resource adequacy. These activities fall squarely within the states' exclusive jurisdiction. Id. To maintain this balance, FERC's final rule should explicitly state that it does not apply to utility/customer interconnections involving retail service, even when those retail loads are large in magnitude.

Cost recovery for upgrades that serve retail load growth should remain within state regulators' ratemaking authority. Assigning such costs under federal tariffs could lead to jurisdictional conflicts and undermine established retail cost recovery mechanisms. FERC should clarify that cost-allocation rules developed in this proceeding will apply only to transmission-level network upgrades (as defined by FERC's Seven-Factor Test) associated with wholesale, not retail, transactions.

The IEA supports FERC's commitment to improving the interconnection process for large loads so long as it does so in a manner that preserves the jurisdictional framework established by Congress and affirmed by the courts. The IEA submits that a cooperative federal–state approach will ensure that large-load interconnections occur efficiently, reliably, and lawfully — promoting economic growth while maintaining regulatory boundaries.

Recognize that states are proactively and effectively addressing large load customer challenges, including transmission interconnections. Explicitly preserve state authority over all retail service. Ensure retail cost recovery remains under state jurisdiction. In addition, the IEA respectfully urges the FERC to continue to focus its efforts on RTO queue reform and encouraging needed transmission investment.

letters.desc: The KCC consistently argues that an unprecedented federal jurisdictional grab is not the right response to large load growth. It contends existing state-federal boundaries are workable, that the ANOPR fails to analyze the full scope of jurisdictional issues, and that certain reform principles could allow large loads to bypass state-franchised utilities in non-restructured states.
quotes: the ANOPR proposes a process that does not address the heart of the issues
the KCC takes issue with the conclusion that an unprecedented expansion of federal jurisdiction is necessary to address these important issues
the appropriate response involves adherence to the well-established divide between state and federal jurisdiction and a commitment to cooperative federalism
This principle suggests that large load customers have a right to directly interconnect to the FERC-regulated grid that trumps state laws regarding retail choice and certificated service territories.

FERC should expressly reject any proposals that allow large load customers to bypass retail utilities in non-restructured states in order to purchase power directly from a wholesale market or an independent generator.

the ANOPR provides no details on implementation. Given the magnitude of the proposed expansion of federal jurisdiction, FERC should take care to fully identify and analyze the relevant issues and avoid relying on unsupported statements about the ANOPR's impact on state jurisdiction

letters.desc: LPPC argues FERC's authority reaches only transmission interconnection, not the terms of retail service, generation cost allocation, or retail wheeling. Asserting jurisdiction over bundled retail transmission would create unintended obligations to regulate retail rates and would conflict with FPA sections 201 and 212(h).
quotes: LPPC asks that this be accomplished while respecting the role reserved under the Federal Power Act ("FPA") to state authorities over retail service, of which large load is an increasing component.

FERC should clarify that if it proceeds with a NOPR, a proposed rule would be limited to the terms of transmission interconnection. The Commission does not have authority to: (1) establish the terms and conditions of retail service to data centers, including the assessment of up-front generation costs to load and the nature of contractual commitments large load may be asked to make; or (2) mandate transmission service to end use customers (retail wheeling).

Further than this, jurisdiction under the FPA for the Commission to control the terms of large load interconnection is far from clear. A declaration that the Commission has jurisdiction over the transmission component of bundled retail sales is a questionable matter, and would have the likely unintended consequence of the Commission taking charge of the transmission cost component of retail sales rates, meaningfully diminishing state-based authority over retail rates.

LPPC asks the Commission to clarify that the ANOPR's disclaimer reserving authority to states encompasses not only rates for direct retail sales but also the ability of Load Serving Entities ("LSEs") to assess the cost of new generation needed to serve large data centers at the outset of service, and to require contractual commitments of specified length to assure cost recovery.

The Commission should expressly hold that its intention is not to preempt the exercise of state authority over the terms of retail service to large load, including the allocation of generation, distribution upgrade costs, retail contract length, and security requirements.

FERC does not have the authority under the FPA to mandate the provision of transmission service to end use customers, a service known as retail wheeling. FPA section 212(h) ("Prohibition on mandatory retail wheeling and sham wholesale transactions") stipulates that "[n]o order issued under this chapter shall be conditioned upon or require the transmission of electric energy: (1) directly to an ultimate consumer; or (2) to, or for the benefit of an entity if such electric energy would be sold by such entity directly to an ultimate consumers...."

This is unnecessary, and inconsistent with planning and operation for retail service, of which large load is a component. The impetus in Order No. 2003 for granting interconnecting generators the opportunity to build out the transmission grid lay in concern that utilities may have a business interest in dragging their feet in providing an interconnection. This is not the case with respect to new retail load, where transmission owning utilities have an obligation to plan, build, and operate facilities under state/local oversight.

letters.desc: LPPC and aligned parties oppose FERC's assertion of jurisdiction over large load interconnections, particularly over retail service terms, cost allocation, and retail wheeling. The council expresses concerns that FERC lacks authority under the Federal Power Act to mandate these interconnections, especially where transmission remains bundled with retail sales, and calls for FERC to clarify it will not mandate retail wheeling under section 210(h).
quotes: LPPC expressed support for the objective articulated by the Department of Energy ("DOE") of a consistent, nationwide approach to large load interconnection. However, LPPC asked that this be accomplished while respecting the role reserved under the Federal Power Act ("FPA") to state authorities over retail service, of which large load is an increasing component.

Concerns that LPPC voiced in its initial comments regarding the scope of FERC's authority to mandate large load interconnections as proposed in the ANOPR have been echoed by a broad cross-section of parties in this docket, including the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners ("NARUC"), the Edison Electric Institute ("EEI"), the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association ("NRECA"), the American Public Power Association ("APPA") and the overwhelming majority of commenting state commissions.

In its comments, LPPC urged the Commission, should it adopt a rule in this docket, to eschew any intention to interfere with the terms and conditions of retail service, including contractual terms and the assessment and allocation of the cost of generation needed to serve large loads.
Further, LPPC asked the Commission to clarify that its intention is not to mandate retail wheeling, as would be prohibited by Federal Power Act ("FPA") section 210(h).

In addition, LPPC cautioned that the Commission's assertion of authority over retail interconnections where transmission remains bundled with retail sales is questionable, and fraught with potential unintended consequences as to the scope of responsibility over retail transmission that the assertion of this jurisdiction would entail.

Rather than unilaterally imposing federal jurisdiction on these interconnections, FERC should pursue a cooperative approach – potentially developing voluntary best practices with states and other novel approaches to meet the moment – without undermining state authority or established statutory frameworks.

letters.org: Louisiana Public Service CommissionMississippi Public Service Commission
letters.desc: The commissions argue the ANOPR intrudes on exclusive state authority over retail load interconnection, resource adequacy, distribution, and planning. They contend FERC has never before claimed jurisdiction over retail load interconnections and should not do so here, especially without evidence of a problem. Even where technical federal jurisdiction exists, cooperative federalism requires restraint.
quotes: the proposed implementation of that goal raises jurisdictional, reliability, resource adequacy, transparency, planning, and cost allocation concerns

Louisiana and Mississippi have not had any issues associated with the delay of the interconnection of large loads, and FERC should be mindful that any rules adopted could unintentionally result in delays, instead of acceleration of the desired interconnections
The ANOPR may be a solution in search of a problem.
the rule should not apply to any transmission owner or transmission provider in the absence of a demonstration that large load interconnections are being met with significant delays

The ANOPR asserts, without offering any evidence that large load interconnection is unreasonable incumbered, that federal jurisdiction is needed to timely interconnect end-use retail customers, which is traditionally within the purview of retail regulators.

the interconnection process accomplishes little without actions to evaluate and approve any generation, distribution and intrastate transmission facilities needed to maintain reliability and resource adequacy – all matters that are within the exclusive jurisdiction of retail regulators

This expansion of federal jurisdiction is not needed in MISO South and SPP regions, the members of which mainly consist of vertically integrated utilities and cooperatives, and it is not needed in Louisiana and Mississippi.

Even if the FERC technically is granted jurisdiction over large load interconnections to the interstate transmission system, it should refrain from exercising that jurisdiction in locations where it is not needed under principles of cooperative federalism.
Giving FERC jurisdiction over the load interconnection as if it were a standalone issue would hamper the efficient planning and development of these projects.

letters.desc: The Maryland PSC argues that large load interconnection falls under state, not federal, jurisdiction under the FPA. It contends the generator-interconnection analogy is flawed because large loads withdraw rather than inject power, their connections qualify as distribution facilities under Order No. 888, and FERC asserting jurisdiction risks litigation that would delay reform goals.
quotes: Achievement of the ANOPR's intended objective need not require the Commission to attempt to assert jurisdiction over entities and processes that otherwise fall under state jurisdiction.

The proposed ANOPR blurs this jurisdictional line by "asserting jurisdiction over the interconnection of large loads to the transmission system," where states have historically exercised their jurisdiction.

large load customers are end-use customers that apply for interconnection service in order to purchase electricity at retail for their own consumption. They are not directly connected to the bulk power system–that is, their physical connection is to the low-voltage side of a substation, and their permitting and construction are strictly state and local matters.

The ANOPR premises the Commission's jurisdiction over large load interconnections on the analogy it makes to generator interconnections. This comparison is fundamentally flawed: a generator interconnection involves connecting a resource that injects electric power into the grid to meet the system's electrical demand. In contrast, large load interconnection involves connecting a facility that withdraws power from the grid.

the Maryland PSC cautions the Commission that states are likely to challenge whether FERC can properly exercise jurisdiction over the interconnection of large load. The Maryland PSC believes a jurisdictional dispute over load interconnection would be counterproductive to all parties' interests and should be avoided.

the Maryland legislature has established that a "large load customer" is a commercial or industrial customer (for retail electric service) that "has or is projected to have an aggregate monthly demand of at least 100 MW…." Where the ANOPR would prescribe new standards and requirements on large load customers that exceed the 20 MW threshold—a much lower qualifying threshold—the Maryland PSC is concerned that if FERC were to exercise jurisdiction over load, these inconsistencies in these large load definitions would create confusion in the regulatory space
